solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Lasso part of train?

definitions.meaning: a rope loop thrown to catch cattle, so playfully a catcher of cows
the metal frame on the front of a locomotive that pushes obstacles off the track

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether a cowboy's rope counts as a piece of railway equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is a whimsical literal reading: a lasso is what a cowboy uses to catch cows.
explanation.definitionFit: On American locomotives the frame fixed at the front to clear livestock from the rails carries this name; a lasso literally does that catching job.

clue.text: Fancy playing Ace when holding King

indicators.note: holding means the shuffled letters keep the king letter inside
playing means the letters of ace are moved about

parts.note: K is the abbreviation for king in cards and chess

explanation.surface: A card player feels tempted to lead the ace while keeping the king.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing' turns ACE into CAE, and 'holding' puts K inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A fancy is a small iced cake, as in a box of fondant fancies.

clue.text: Almost cry about topless lout appearing twice in beach resort

indicators.note: almost means the cry word loses its last letter

parts.note: to wail is to cry

indicators.note: says the turned piece is written two times in a row
about means the trimmed lout word is turned round
topless means the lout word loses its first letter

parts.note: oik is British slang for a lout

explanation.surface: A near-tearful scene as a shirtless yob turns up twice at a seaside resort.
explanation.walkthrough: OIK is British slang for a boorish lout. 'about' turns the topless lout round before 'appearing twice' doubles it.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous beach on Oahu, in Honolulu, Hawaii, is a classic seaside holiday spot.

clue.text: Some uplift when sweltering and not quite ready to fight?

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
sweltering means very hot

indicators.note: not quite means the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a soldier serving in the forces is ready to fight

explanation.surface: Asks whether a sweaty, unfit recruit feels a little encouraged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' drops the Y of IN THE ARMY.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for a boost or stimulus that revives something, so a bit of encouragement or uplift.

clue.text: Study poetry for talk

parts.note: to con is an old verb for to study
verse is poetry

explanation.surface: Someone weighs reading poems against chatting.
explanation.walkthrough: CON for study is a crossword staple, meaning to learn by heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To converse is to hold a conversation, to chat with someone.

clue.text: Concentrate when court goes unused

indicators.note: goes means the court letters leave the concentrate word

parts.note: an extract is a concentrate, as in vanilla extract

explanation.surface: Suggests focusing hard while a tennis court sits empty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Concentrate' looks like a verb but is the noun, an extract; 'goes' removes CT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extra is spare or surplus, left over and not used.

clue.text: Dandy with insert of 'Beryl's Final Fall'

indicators.note: says a letter is put into the middle of the dandy word

parts.note: a dandy is a fop, a man vain about his clothes

indicators.note: Beryl's final means the last letter of the name Beryl

explanation.surface: Reads like the title of a melodrama about a lady named Beryl, put into a comic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with insert of' puts the last letter of Beryl, L, inside FOP. 'Dandy' also suggests the British children's comic of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: To fall flat, as a show or venture does, is to fail completely; a fall in this sense is a failure.

clue.text: Guard in place to go and whip missing knight

parts.note: loo is British slang for a toilet, the place to go

indicators.note: missing means the knight letter is taken from the whip word

parts.note: a knout is a Russian scourge or whip
N is the chess abbreviation for knight

explanation.surface: A sentry stationed at a toilet with a whip but no knight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place to go' is a euphemism for a toilet. 'missing' takes N from KNOUT, leaving KOUT.
explanation.definitionFit: A lookout is a person posted to watch for danger, a sentry or guard.

clue.text: 13 state journalists going round gambling without limits

definitions.note: the state of being what the answer to 13 down describes, a noun

indicators.note: going round means the journalists word wraps round the trimmed letters

parts.note: the press are journalists collectively

indicators.note: without limits means the gambling word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: betting is gambling

explanation.surface: Reporters cover a state that has legalised gambling in a limited way.
explanation.walkthrough: 13 is the answer to 13 down, ATTRACTIVE; the state of being so is the definition. 'without limits' leaves ETTIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Prettiness is the quality of being good-looking, a state of being pleasant to look at.

clue.text: Man seen in 'Some Like It Hot'

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Points to a character spotted in the classic Billy Wilder comedy film.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft took 'Man seen' as the definition, but 'seen in' is only a link; the man is the definition. 'Some' doubles as the start of the film title and the signal that letters are taken from what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A common male first name, so any bearer of it is an example of a man.

clue.text: Ottoman? He moved out

indicators.note: moved means the letters of the two words are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: Asks about a padded footstool, then reports that a man changed house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moved' reworks the letters of OTTOMAN and HE together; 'Ottoman' looks like a reference to the Turkish empire or a piece of furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is out when you call is away from their house, the idiom used on a doorstep.

clue.text: Retro hit with leader of artificial men travelling across time?

definitions.text: Retro hit with leader of artificial men travelling across time?

indicators.note: across means the reshuffled letters sit over and around the time letter
travelling means these letters move into a new order
leader of means the first letter of artificial

explanation.surface: Describes a classic film in which artificial men travel through time.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the 1984 film, in which a cyborg is sent back from the future; 'travelling' shuffles the pool and 'across' puts T inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1984 science-fiction film is now a retro hit about an android assassin who travels back in time.

clue.text: Suffering similarly, like shipmates

definitions.meaning: sharing the same predicament as others
literally, sailors who travel together on one vessel

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition reads the idiom literally: shipmates are all aboard one vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means sharing a difficult situation with others, and taken word for word it describes a crew aboard one vessel.

clue.text: Pleasant-looking area in home without roof

indicators.note: in says the area word goes inside the trimmed home word
in a down clue the roof is the top letter, so the home word loses its first letter

parts.note: native means home, as in one's home country or native land
a tract is an area of land

explanation.surface: Describes a pleasant room in a house that has lost its roof.
explanation.walkthrough: 'home' is the adjective, as in one's home country; in a down clue the roof is the first letter, which 'without roof' removes.
explanation.definitionFit: Attractive means appealing to the eye, which is what being nice to look at amounts to.

clue.text: Superlatively poor trial involving hotel and pub

indicators.note: involving means the trial word takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: a trial is a test
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
an inn is a pub

explanation.surface: Suggests a shoddy trial that dragged in a hotel and a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Superlatively' signals the -est form: poor here means weak or slight, as in a thin excuse.
explanation.definitionFit: Thin can mean feeble or meagre, as with a thin argument, so the superlative is the poorest of all.

clue.text: One might dig it lots? All but the finish

parts.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal or sex

indicators.note: says the lots word loses its final letter

parts.note: tons is informal for lots

explanation.surface: Wonders if someone would enjoy something a great deal, then says the end is missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' is a long-standing crossword and slang euphemism for SEX; 'All but the finish' drops the S of TONS. 'dig' seems to mean like but is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A church officer who traditionally looks after the graveyard and digs the graves.

clue.text: Clear chemists to replace oxygen in milk

indicators.note: to replace means the chemists swap in where the oxygen letter was
in places the swap inside the milk word

parts.note: to milk something is to exploit it
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
setter's slip: chemists is the usual cue for ICI, Imperial Chemical Industries, but only its first two letters fit here

explanation.surface: Pharmacists swap oxygen into milk, which reads like a lab procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue is flawed as published: chemists means ICI (Imperial Chemical Industries), and putting all three letters in place of the O gives one I too many. The blog flagged it and the Telegraph later changed the clue online.
explanation.definitionFit: Explicit means stated plainly and leaving no doubt, which is what being clear means.

clue.text: Royals clash over indications of sympathy

indicators.note: over in a down-style sense means the clash word is turned around

parts.note: to jar is to clash
ahs are sounds of sympathy

explanation.surface: Members of a royal family argue while others make sympathetic noises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' reverses JAR to RAJ.
explanation.definitionFit: Indian princes or kings held this title, so they are royals.

clue.text: Dream reindeer regularly take sleigh without permission?

parts.note: a dream, something delightful, is a joy

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of reindeer is taken

explanation.surface: A Christmas fantasy of the reindeer taking Santa's sleigh out for a spin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the odd letters of reindeer.
explanation.definitionFit: To take a vehicle for a thrill ride without the owner's consent; a sleigh is a whimsical vehicle, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Test locations losing account for prototypes

parts.note: an exam is a test

indicators.note: losing means the locations word sheds the account letters

parts.note: places are locations

explanation.surface: Exam halls that lost their funding being treated as models for others.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing' removes AC from PLACES to leave PLES.
explanation.definitionFit: Prototypes are models or instances set up as patterns to follow, in the sense of setting a good model.

clue.text: Left sat around at home, needing good following long-term

indicators.note: following means the good letter comes after the rest
around means the letters of sat are moved about

parts.note: in means at home, as in staying in

explanation.surface: Someone left sitting about at home needing a good long spell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' rearranges the three letters of sat; 'following' places G at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Lasting means enduring or durable, persisting over a long period.

clue.text: Claim sand, say, shifting around new overseas territory

indicators.note: around means the reshuffled letters wrap round the new letter
shifting means the letters of these words move into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone claims a sandy beach in a far-off British territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shifting' rearranges CLAIMSANDSAY, and 'around' places N inside the result.
explanation.definitionFit: The Caribbean island group is one of the British Overseas Territories.

clue.text: Ace cast with this opening passage could get reaction

indicators.note: cast means letters thrown together and rearranged, so the ace letters plus the answer's make the final word

explanation.surface: A musician says a well-played opening would draw a response.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite: shuffle ACE together with the answer and you get REACTION. 'with this' refers to the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: An intro is the introductory section of a song or piece, its opening passage.

clue.text: Outdo George?

definitions.meaning: George ..., the Northern Irish footballer of Manchester United

explanation.walkthrough: George Best was a Northern Ireland and Manchester United footballer of the 1960s and 70s.
explanation.definitionFit: To outdo a rival is to beat them, and the surname belongs to the famous footballer George.

clue.text: Barking welcomes parent using dialect

indicators.note: welcomes means the barking word takes the parent word in

parts.note: barking, short for barking mad, means crazy or idiotic
ma is a mother, a parent

explanation.surface: A mad person receives a mother who speaks in a regional dialect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' is British slang for mad, not a dog's noise or the London suburb.
explanation.definitionFit: Speech full of natural local expressions and turns of phrase is idiomatic, the way native speakers use language.

clue.text: Rubbish journey east

parts.note: a trip is a journey
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A dismissive verdict on a trip to the east.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripe is informal for nonsense or worthless talk, the same as rubbish.

clue.text: Half of West Country see about big cheese

indicators.note: half of means only the first three letters of the see's name are used

parts.note: Exeter, a city in Devon in South West England, is the seat of a diocese, a see
C, for circa, is the abbreviation for about

explanation.surface: Half of the West Country looks on as a top boss arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'see' is a bishop's diocese, not the verb. 'Half of' keeps EXE from EXETER.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for executive, a senior manager, matching the informal term for an important boss.

clue.text: Straight-talking banker? Correct

parts.note: a river is a banker since it has banks; the Forth is a Scottish river
right means correct

explanation.surface: Asks whether a frank banker gets it right.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banker' is crossword shorthand for a river, here the Forth in Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A forthright person is direct and frank, saying plainly what they think.
